statutory.question: Does the conduct described fall within 5318(g)?
statutory.answer: No. 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) suspicious activity reporting requirements are not triggered on these facts alone.
statutory.label: neutral
statutory.reasoning: 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) authorizes/mandates the Secretary (via regulation) to require a “financial institution” to report “any suspicious transaction relevant to a possible violation of law or regulation,” and provides related safe-harbor and confidentiality provisions. Element-by-element: (1) Covered reporter: § 5318(g) applies to “financial institutions” (as defined/implemented by BSA regulations). The fact pattern describes Entity SYN_352c41a3 as a business/MSB, but it does not state that it is acting as the reporting financial institution subject to SAR rules (e.g., a regulated MSB with SAR obligations) versus merely a customer whose transactions are being observed; this is insufficient to determine applicability. (2) Suspicious transaction: § 5318(g) hinges on a transaction being “suspicious” and “relevant to a possible violation of law or regulation.” The listed ACH/wire/card/cash transactions (amounts mostly $7k–$31k) do not include facts indicating illegality, structuring intent, fraud, sanctions evasion, or other red flags beyond volume; thus the record does not establish that any transaction is “suspicious” within § 5318(g). (3) Reporting duty/trigger: § 5318(g) duties are implemented by regulations (thresholds, timing, categories), but no regulatory trigger facts (e.g., known/suspected criminal proceeds, attempts to evade BSA requirements, or other specified SAR criteria) are provided. Therefore, while § 5318(g) suspicious activity reporting requirements could apply in general to a covered MSB, the facts are insufficient to conclude the conduct falls within § 5318(g).
